content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses identify the sword's primary Christian symbolic meaning as the Word of God — Scripture/God's speech as a penetrating spiritual weapon of truth, conviction, and discernment (Eph 6:17; Heb 4:12; Rev 1:16; 19:15). Widely acknowledged alternatives include divine judgment/wrath (Isa 34; Ezek 21; Rev 19:15), war/violence and death (Rev 6:4), civil authority (Rom 13:4), gospel-provoked division (Matt 10:34), sorrow (Luke 2:35), and martyrdom.","book_summary":"The book defines the sword as 'war and the word of judgment' — the great sword given the red horse's rider that takes peace from the earth (Rev 6:4) and the flaming sword guarding the way to the tree of life (Gen 3:24). It foregrounds warfare and judicial exclusion rather than the edifying/discerning Word wielded by believers.","consensus_core_identification":"The Word of God functioning as a spiritual weapon — living, penetrating truth that convicts, discerns, and (secondarily) executes judgment; with divine judgment and literal war as recognized secondary senses.","book_core_identification":"War and the word of judgment — the sword as instrument that removes peace from the earth and as God's judicial word/barrier guarding the way (exclusion from Eden).","core_relation":"COMPATIBLE_OVERLAP","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book demotes or drops the consensus's dominant sense (the Word as the believer's spiritual weapon of truth and discernment — Eph 6:17; Heb 4:12) and elevates two of the consensus's listed alternatives — war/violence (Rev 6:4) and divine judgment (Gen 3:24) — to primary status, while retaining a 'word' element only in its judicial function ('word of judgment'). Cases the consensus centers (conviction, sanctifying discernment, spiritual warfare defense) are excluded from the core; cases the consensus treats as secondary (taking peace from the earth, judgment/exclusion from Eden) become central.","material_contradiction":"None strictly — the consensus itself notes that word and judgment merge in Revelation and lists war and judgment as common senses. The book does not deny that the sword can signify God's word; it recasts it as specifically the word of judgment joined with war, rather than replacing the referent with an incompatible one.","rationale":"The book's identification is not novel: both of its components (war and divine judgment) appear as 'common' alternatives in every consensus response, and 'word of judgment' preserves a recognizable slice of the consensus's central Word-of-God referent (cf. Rev 19:15 read as Christ's word of judgment). But the book materially re-centers the symbol, narrowing the 'word' component to its judicial function and pairing it with war, thereby rejecting the default gloss (Scripture as the believer's convicting, discerning weapon) as the primary meaning. This is a genuine boundary and emphasis disagreement without contradiction of referent, fitting REFINED with a partial reclassification of covered cases.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT: the consensus's central identification — the Word of God as the Spirit's sword that believers wield (Eph 6:17) — is effectively displaced by 'war,' and neither printed citation (Rev 6:4; Gen 3:24) mentions a 'word' at all, suggesting the book has replaced the referent rather than refined its boundary. The 'word of judgment' phrase may be doing less bridging work than a REFINED verdict assumes.","confidence":"medium"}
